note: Question types for premise excavation. Ordinary requirements questions ('who is the user, what are the constraints, what does success look like') are premise-preserving: they refine the idea the person already has. Each family here is designed to expose something the brief takes for granted. Ask one at a time, in the user's language, phrased for their actual brief - never paste a template phrasing verbatim.

families.label: The premise nobody states
families.purpose: Surface the assumption so basic that neither of you has said it out loud.
prompts: Everything in this brief assumes {X} is a single thing that exists in one place. Is that actually required, or just how it has always been done?
What has to be true about the world for this to make sense at all?
families.listens_for: Hesitation, or an answer that starts with 'well, obviously'. That is the load-bearing premise.
families.anti_pattern: Asking what the requirements are. Requirements sit on top of premises; you want the layer underneath.

families.label: The version you would hate
families.purpose: Get the user's own ban list before they see yours.
prompts: Describe the version of this that you would be embarrassed to show anyone. What makes it embarrassing?
If someone else shipped this next month and you rolled your eyes, what would they have built?
families.listens_for: Specific names and concrete features, not adjectives. Push until you get one you could recognize on sight.
families.anti_pattern: Asking what they want to avoid in the abstract. 'Nothing generic' is not usable; 'not another dashboard with three KPI cards' is.

families.label: Success under a different definition
families.purpose: Break the metric the brief silently optimizes for.
prompts: Suppose the number you would normally measure is unavailable forever. How would you know this worked?
What would make this a success for someone who never uses it?
families.listens_for: A second, more honest goal hiding behind the stated one.
families.anti_pattern: Asking for KPIs. That confirms the existing metric instead of testing it.

families.label: The constraint, inverted
families.purpose: Test whether a limit is a fact or an inherited habit.
prompts: You said {constraint}. What would this become if that were reversed rather than merely relaxed?
Which constraint here would you defend hardest, and what would this become if we spent one minute assuming it is wrong?
families.listens_for: Whether the answer changes the shape of the thing or only its size. Only shape counts.
families.anti_pattern: Asking to remove constraints. Removal produces fantasy; inversion produces a different design.

families.label: Who this is not for
families.purpose: Find the people the concept is quietly addressed to, and the ones it acts on without asking.
prompts: Who is affected by this without ever choosing to use it?
Who should look at this and correctly conclude it is not for them?
families.listens_for: 'Everyone' means the audience has not been chosen. Keep going.
families.anti_pattern: Asking for a target persona. That names a buyer, not a boundary.

families.label: What must stay impossible
families.purpose: Every real design forbids something; a design that forbids nothing is a wish list.
prompts: What should this make harder or outright impossible, on purpose?
What is the thing you never want a user of this to be able to do, even when they ask nicely?
families.listens_for: A real refusal with a cost attached. 'We'd never do anything bad' is not one.
families.anti_pattern: Asking about non-goals. Non-goals are things you skipped; this is about things you actively prevent.

families.label: The graveyard
families.purpose: Ground the work in what has already been tried and what killed it.
prompts: Who has tried something in this neighbourhood, and what specifically killed it?
Have you tried a version of this before? What did you learn that you have not written down?
families.listens_for: Causes of death. If the same cause is still present, the new idea inherits it.
families.anti_pattern: Asking about competitors. You want post-mortems, not a landscape.

families.label: What it commits people to
families.purpose: Expose the ongoing duty the concept creates for someone.
prompts: Once this exists, who has to keep doing something forever for it to keep working?
What does using this once oblige a person to do afterwards?
families.listens_for: Maintenance, moderation, refills, re-consent, apology paths. This is where concepts die quietly.
families.anti_pattern: Asking about cost in money only. The expensive part is usually a recurring human duty.

families.label: Where this already exists under another name
families.purpose: Find the domain that already solved the structure of this problem for other reasons.
prompts: Outside your field entirely, who deals with this same structure - and what do they call it?
If a harbour master, a hospice nurse, or a tax office handled this, what would they already have in place?
families.listens_for: A borrowed mechanism with real detail attached, not a metaphor.
families.anti_pattern: Asking for analogies. An analogy decorates; a borrowed mechanism does work.

families.label: How it ends
families.purpose: Design the end state, which is where most concepts are silently unfinished.
prompts: What does this look like when it is finished, abandoned, or dead? Who cleans up?
How would someone leave this, and what do they take with them?
families.listens_for: Whether an ending exists at all. If nothing can end, nothing can be committed to.
families.anti_pattern: Asking about the roadmap. A roadmap is growth; this is termination.

families.label: The scale where it breaks
families.purpose: Locate the threshold at which the concept becomes a different thing.
prompts: At a hundred times the size, what stops being true?
At a hundredth the size, what becomes pointless?
families.listens_for: A threshold with a number attached. That threshold is usually the real design boundary.
families.anti_pattern: Asking whether it scales. That invites a yes.

families.label: The administrative half
families.purpose: Force the paperwork, because extraordinary things become real when they become routine.
prompts: What is the dullest recurring task this creates - the form, the queue, the monthly reconciliation?
Who has to sign off, and what do they need to see before they will?
families.listens_for: The first genuinely concrete detail of the concept. Often the best material in the session.
families.anti_pattern: Skipping this because it is unglamorous. This family produces more usable specificity than any other.
